name: Functional and Tributary Areas
hook: Follow the trips, not just the boundary.
parts: Functional areas are linked by activities; tributary areas are served by an urban center.
Commuting, shopping and medical trips connect places beyond city limits.
Different activities produce different, overlapping boundaries.
Someone may live outside the city but work and shop inside it.

mnemonic.text: Function follows FLOWS. Picture commuting, shopping and hospital trips crossing a city border.
lines: Picture commuting, shopping and hospital trips crossing a city border.

fullParts: Functional areas are connected by shared activities; tributary areas are surrounding territories served by or oriented toward an urban center.
Commuting, trade, medical services, media markets and other flows link a city to places beyond its administrative boundary.
Different functions produce different, sometimes overlapping boundaries, so a city’s influence can extend far into its region.
Central Place Theory explains service hinterlands, while functional definitions help analyze metropolitan transport and employment.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A city’s real reach extends beyond its official border. Trips link functional areas; an urban center serves surrounding tributary areas.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You live outside city limits but commute into the city and use its hospital.

name: Von Thunen Model
hook: Farms must pay delivery costs too.
parts: Von Thünen explains farming patterns around a market.
Farmers compare land rent, production costs and transport costs.
Different products can afford different locations, creating rings under the model’s assumptions.
A product costly to transport has a reason to locate near the market.

mnemonic.text: Farm rings have delivery bills. Market in the middle; farms around it.
lines: Market in the middle; farms around it.

fullParts: Von Thünen’s model explains agricultural land-use patterns around a central market.
Farmers compare production costs, land rent and transport costs; uses with higher transport burdens or returns may bid more for nearby land.
Under simplified conditions, competing rent bids create rings of different agricultural uses around the market.
Its land–transport trade-off anticipates urban bid-rent models such as Alonso–Muth–Mills.

visuals.caption: Rings around one market: transport costs help sort farms by location.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Von Thünen explains rings of farming around a market: farmers balance land, production and transport costs.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Products that are expensive to transport have a reason to locate closer to the market.

name: Central Place Theory
hook: Buy milk nearby; travel farther for rare services.
parts: Central Place Theory explains why settlements form a service hierarchy.
Everyday shops need a small customer area; specialized services need a larger one.
Small centers are numerous; large centers are fewer and farther apart.
Convenience stores are common; major specialist hospitals are less common.

mnemonic.text: Milk nearby; rare specialist farther away. Everyday needs → many small centers.
lines: Milk nearby; rare specialist farther away.

fullParts: Central Place Theory explains a hierarchy of settlements that supply goods and services to surrounding areas.
Services need enough customers to survive, while customers will travel only a limited distance to obtain them.
Everyday services appear in many small centers; specialized services support fewer, larger and more widely spaced centers.
It explains service areas between settlements, whereas Alonso–Muth–Mills explains residential location within a city.

visuals.caption: Small centers serve nearby customers; larger centers offer rarer services. Hexagons represent idealized market areas.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Common services need small customer areas; rare services need larger ones. This helps explain many small centers and fewer large centers.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Many neighborhoods have grocery stores; only a few places have specialist hospitals.

name: Sector/Multiple Nuclei Model
hook: Pizza slices versus several centers.
parts: Hoyt’s Sector Model follows corridors; the Multiple Nuclei Model has several centers.
Transport routes shape sectors, while related activities cluster into different centers.
Cities need not grow as rings around one downtown.
Picture wedges along railways versus separate shopping, industrial and office centers.

mnemonic.text: Sector = pizza. Nuclei = egg yolks. Pizza slices = wedges; several yolks = several centers.
lines: Pizza slices = wedges; several yolks = several centers.

fullParts: Hoyt’s Sector Model describes development in corridors or wedges; Harris and Ullman’s Multiple Nuclei Model describes several specialized centers.
Transport routes shape sectors, while compatible activities cluster and incompatible uses separate to form different nuclei.
These models explain urban patterns that do not fit simple concentric rings around a single downtown.
They connect transport and land use to polycentric development, contrasting with the simplest monocentric model.

visuals.caption: SECTORS = wedges extending outward along transport routes.

studyBlocks.label: Sector model
studyBlocks.text: Land uses grow outward in wedges, often along transport routes.

studyBlocks.label: Multiple nuclei
studyBlocks.text: Different activities cluster around several centers.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Industry along a railway versus separate industrial, shopping and office centers.

studyBlocks.label: The distinction
studyBlocks.text: WEDGES describe corridors; NUCLEI describe centers. Neither requires rings around one CBD.

name: Alonso-Muth-Mills (Intracity) Model
hook: Near the CBD: less commuting, more rent.
parts: AMM explains housing choices within one city（城内）.
People trade housing costs against commuting costs.
Homes farther from the center usually offer cheaper space but longer trips.
Think: small downtown flat versus large suburban home. Rosen–Roback compares different cities.

mnemonic.text: AMM: one city, one seesaw. Near the center: rent ↑, commute ↓.

fullParts: The Alonso–Muth–Mills model explains residential location and land rents within a city, initially assuming jobs in one central business district.
Households trade higher central housing costs against the cost of commuting from cheaper land farther away.
Under its assumptions, rents and residential density generally decline with distance from the center.
It is an intracity model; Rosen–Roback instead compares wages, rents and amenities across cities.

visuals.caption: Near the center, access is valuable and bids for land are higher. This is related bid-rent logic, not the full AMM model.

studyBlocks.label: The question
studyBlocks.text: Where should you live WITHIN one city?

studyBlocks.label: The trade-off
studyBlocks.text: Closer to the center: higher housing costs, lower commuting costs. Farther out: the reverse under the model’s assumptions.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Small downtown flat versus a larger suburban home with a longer commute.

studyBlocks.label: Don’t mix up
studyBlocks.text: AMM = within a city. Rosen–Roback = between cities.

name: Rosen-Roback (Intercity) Model
hook: Different cities, the same three questions.
parts: Rosen–Roback explains choices between cities（城际）.
People weigh wages, rents and amenities: income, housing cost and quality of life.
High wages may be offset by high rent.
Someone may accept lower pay to live near the beach. AMM stays within one city.

mnemonic.text: Rosen–Roback → ROAM. Between cities: wages − rent + amenities. A memory balance, not an exact equation.
lines: Between cities: wages − rent + amenities. A memory balance, not an exact equation.

fullParts: The Rosen–Roback model explains differences in wages and housing costs between cities through spatial equilibrium.
Mobile households balance wages, housing costs and amenities, while firms weigh labor and land costs against productivity.
High rents can reflect productive employment, desirable amenities or both; attractive places may offer lower real incomes.
Unlike the intracity Alonso–Muth–Mills model, it asks why people choose different metropolitan areas.

studyBlocks.label: The question
studyBlocks.text: Which CITY should you choose?

studyBlocks.label: The trade-off
studyBlocks.text: Compare wages, housing costs and amenities. Higher pay can be offset by higher rent.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You accept lower pay to live near the beach because you value that amenity.

studyBlocks.label: Don’t mix up
studyBlocks.text: Rosen–Roback = between cities. AMM = within one city.

name: Agglomeration
hook: Being nearby can make work easier.
parts: Agglomeration brings benefits from clustering people and firms.
They share resources, find workers and exchange ideas more easily.
Productivity may rise, but so can rents and congestion.
A design firm benefits from nearby clients and talent, while paying more for space.

mnemonic.text: Agglomeration → a GLOB of firms. Nearness helps SHARE, MATCH and LEARN.
lines: Nearness helps SHARE, MATCH and LEARN.

fullParts: Agglomeration is the concentration of people and economic activities that produces benefits from proximity.
Nearby firms and workers can share suppliers and infrastructure, find better matches and exchange knowledge more easily.
These advantages can raise productivity and attract activity, while congestion and high land costs offset some benefits.
Agglomeration explains why cities form; spatial equilibrium explains how higher productivity can be reflected in wages and rents.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: People and firms can benefit from being close together: sharing resources, finding workers and exchanging ideas. This is agglomeration.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A design firm finds clients and skilled workers nearby, but also pays higher rent and faces congestion.

name: Monocentric/Polycentric
hook: Mono = one main center; poly = several.
parts: Monocentric cities have one dominant center; polycentric cities have several important centers.
Transport, land prices and business movement shape these patterns.
Trips need not all lead toward the same downtown.
The course contrasts Chicago’s strong center with Los Angeles’s multiple centers.

mnemonic.text: MONO = one peak. POLY = several. One dominant center versus several important centers.
lines: One dominant center versus several important centers.

fullParts: A monocentric city has one dominant center of employment and activity; a polycentric city has several significant centers.
Transport systems, land costs and the decentralization of firms and services shape the number and strength of centers.
Polycentric development creates more varied commuting patterns than a simple suburb-to-downtown flow.
The course contrasts Chicago’s strong center with Los Angeles’s multiple centers; Multiple Nuclei models help explain the latter.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Monocentric means one dominant center; polycentric means several important centers.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Chicago’s strong center versus Los Angeles’s multiple centers is the course comparison, not an absolute rule.

name: Machine City
hook: Build the roads; you cannot copy the history.
parts: Machine City treats a city as a system that planners can design.
Roads, pipes and parks can be planned.
Chicago also grew through geography, inventions and historical events that cannot simply be copied.
Copying Chicago’s layout would not guarantee another Chicago.

mnemonic.text: A city is not a photocopy. Copy the pipes and roads ≠ copy the history.
lines: A city is not a photocopy.
Copy the pipes and roads ≠ copy the history.

fullParts: Machine City is the idea that a city can be understood and reproduced as a planned, engineered system.
Chicago shows that transport networks, green space and engineering can be deliberately organized.
Yet its rise also depended on geography, early advantages, innovation and historical events that planners cannot simply reproduce.
This limits top-down planning and connects to Lynch’s view of cities as evolving learning ecologies.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A city can be planned like a machine, with roads, pipes and parks working together. But geography and history also shape its growth.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Copy Chicago’s street plan and you still won’t recreate Chicago’s economy.

name: Urbanization without Growth
hook: A bigger urban share is not a bigger paycheck.
parts: Urbanization without growth means more people live in cities without matching income growth.
Rural hardship, urban policies and improved survival can increase the urban share.
Cities may expand while poverty remains.
Moving to a city to escape a drought does not guarantee a productive urban job.

mnemonic.text: Two counters, not one. Urban population share ↑ does not mean income per person ↑.
lines: Urban population share ↑ does not mean income per person ↑.

fullParts: Urbanization without growth means a population becomes more urban without a corresponding rise in income per person.
Safer urban living, urban-biased policies, rural hardship and urban natural population increase can raise the urban share without strong productivity growth.
Cities can expand while poverty persists and industrial employment remains limited.
This challenges treating urbanization as proof of development and connects to rural push and resource-financed consumption cities.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: More people living in cities does not automatically mean higher incomes or better jobs.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: People escape a rural drought by moving to a city, but productive urban jobs may not be waiting.

name: Rural Push/Urban Pull
hook: Push from behind; pull from ahead.
parts: Rural push drives people away from the countryside; urban pull attracts them to cities.
Drought or lost livelihoods can push; jobs and education can pull.
Migration can reflect hardship rather than growing urban prosperity.
Escaping rural unemployment does not mean a good city job is waiting.

mnemonic.text: PUSH behind; PULL ahead. Drought pushes out; city jobs pull in.
lines: Drought pushes out; city jobs pull in.

fullParts: Rural push drives people out of the countryside, while urban pull attracts them toward opportunities in cities.
Drought, conflict or lost rural livelihoods can push migration; jobs, wages, education and services can pull it.
Migration may reflect rural distress rather than expanding productive urban employment.
This helps explain urbanization without growth and why migration alone is not evidence of improving living standards.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Rural PUSH makes people leave the countryside; urban PULL attracts them to a city.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Drought pushes; jobs and education pull. Moving because of hardship does not guarantee a good city job.

name: Malthusian/Solowian Growth
hook: A bigger cake may have more people sharing it.
source: Course growth notes; Jedwab & Vollrath’s Malthusian discussion
parts: In a Malthusian economy, population growth can absorb income gains.
In Solow, more capital raises output per worker but faces diminishing returns.
Sustained long-run growth per person requires technological progress in the standard model.
More total output—or more urban residents—does not automatically mean richer individuals.

mnemonic.text: Malthus = MOUTHS. Solow = SLOWING gains. Population absorbs gains; capital has diminishing returns. Technology sustains growth per person.
lines: Population absorbs gains; capital has diminishing returns. Technology sustains growth per person.

fullParts: Malthusian growth describes gains absorbed by population growth, while Solowian growth distinguishes total output from output per worker.
In a Malthusian economy, more people press against limited resources; in Solow, capital deepening raises output but faces diminishing returns.
Sustained long-run growth per person requires technological progress in the standard Solow model, rather than capital accumulation alone.
This distinction helps explain why a larger urban population does not necessarily mean higher living standards.

studyBlocks.label: Malthus
studyBlocks.text: Population growth can absorb gains in output, keeping income per person low.

studyBlocks.label: Solow
studyBlocks.text: More capital per worker raises output, but each additional unit brings a smaller gain.

studyBlocks.label: Long-run growth
studyBlocks.text: In the standard Solow model, sustained growth per person requires technological progress.

studyBlocks.label: Remember
studyBlocks.text: A bigger population or more total output does not automatically mean richer individuals.

name: Consumption City
hook: Spending resource income is not the same as industrial growth.
source: Jedwab & Vollrath; course notes distinguish the consumer-city usage
parts: A consumption city grows by spending income from resources such as oil.
That money supports shops, restaurants and other local services.
The city can grow without a strong manufacturing economy.
More urban jobs do not necessarily mean higher productivity: urbanization without growth.

mnemonic.text: Oil → spending → services. Picture oil money buying meals and haircuts.
lines: Picture oil money buying meals and haircuts.

fullParts: In Jedwab and Vollrath, a consumption city grows through spending financed by resource income rather than industrial production.
Resource revenues support demand for urban goods and non-tradable services, drawing workers into those activities.
Urbanization can therefore occur without the productivity gains associated with industrialization.
This illustrates urbanization without growth; distinguish it from the consumer-city idea that amenities attract residents.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A consumption city grows by spending resource income, such as oil money, on shops and services. It need not develop strong manufacturing.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Oil income supports restaurants and shops, but urban growth does not guarantee broad productivity growth.

name: Urban Economic Transition
hook: The city changes how it earns a living.
parts: Urban economic transition means a change in a city’s main industries and jobs.
Employment may shift from farming to factories, then services.
Some cities gain new work; others lose the industry they depended on.
A factory closure can hurt the whole surrounding neighborhood.

mnemonic.text: FIELD → FACTORY → OFFICE. Three pictures for changing economic roles.
lines: Three pictures for changing economic roles.

fullParts: Urban economic transition is the changing economic base of cities as employment shifts among agriculture, manufacturing and services.
Industrialization concentrates factories and workers; later deindustrialization and specialization increase the importance of services.
Cities that adapt can grow, while places dependent on a declining industry may lose jobs and population.
Detroit connects this transition to shrinking cities and to the unequal job access examined by Grengs.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A city’s economy changes as its main jobs and industries change. Some places adapt; others lose the work they depend on.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A factory closes: workers lose jobs and nearby shops lose customers.

name: Shrinking Cities
hook: Fewer taxpayers, but the same long roads and pipes.
source: Course shrinking-city notes; Detroit in Grengs
parts: A shrinking city experiences lasting population loss, often with job losses.
Industry decline, outward migration or demographic change reduce demand.
Vacant buildings and a smaller tax base make services harder to maintain.
Detroit connects industrial change to urban decline and unequal job access.

mnemonic.text: Fewer people, the same long pipes. Population and tax base shrink.
lines: Fewer people, the same long pipes.

fullParts: Shrinking cities experience sustained population loss, often accompanied by declining employment and underused urban space.
Deindustrialization, suburbanization, outmigration and demographic change can reduce demand for housing and services.
Vacant buildings and a smaller tax base make it harder to maintain infrastructure and public services.
Detroit links urban economic transition to shrinking cities, showing why population decline can coexist with severe accessibility problems.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A shrinking city loses population over a sustained period, often alongside jobs. Empty buildings and a smaller tax base make services harder to support.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Industrial decline leaves fewer workers, fewer customers and less money to maintain streets.

name: Density
hook: Amount divided by area—not a quality score.
parts: Density counts people, homes or buildings per unit of land.
The result depends on what and where you count.
Higher density can support services, but does not guarantee walkability or good social life.
The same number of buildings can form connected streets or isolated compounds.

mnemonic.text: Density = AMOUNT ÷ AREA. Always name the amount: people, homes or floor space.
lines: Always name the amount: people, homes or floor space.

fullParts: Density is the amount of population, housing or development per unit of land area.
Its value depends on what is counted and the boundary used; the same average can conceal different spatial arrangements.
Higher density can support nearby services and transit, but alone does not reveal connectivity, land-use mix or social experience.
Galster treats density as one of eight sprawl dimensions, while Jacobs links it to other conditions for vitality.

visuals.caption: Picture how much land each home uses. Density measures an amount per unit of area, not a street pattern.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Density means how much is packed into an area: people, homes or floor space. Always ask what is counted and where.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Two equally dense places may feel very different: connected streets versus isolated compounds.

name: Griddedness
hook: Order + straight lines + four-way crossings.
source: Boeing: Off the Grid and Back Again
parts: Griddedness measures how much streets resemble a grid.
Boeing combines orientation order, straightness and four-way intersections.
Connected routes offer more choices than loops and dead ends.
Grid-like neighborhoods have lower car ownership on average; this association alone does not prove causation.

mnemonic.text: A checkerboard has three clues. Orderly directions + straight streets + four-way crossings.
lines: Orderly directions + straight streets + four-way crossings.

fullParts: Griddedness measures how closely a street network resembles a grid through orientation order, straightness and four-way intersections.
Connected routes offer direct paths and alternatives, unlike disconnected loops and cul-de-sacs.
Boeing finds a historical decline and partial return of grids, with more grid-like neighborhoods associated with lower car ownership.
This relates to the design component of the D variables; the association alone does not prove that grids cause less driving.

visuals.caption: Many connected streets and intersections create several possible routes.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Griddedness describes how grid-like a street network is: consistent directions, straight streets and four-way intersections.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A connected grid gives you several routes; loops and dead ends give you fewer choices.

name: “D Variables”
hook: How much? What mix? Which streets? What destinations? How far to transit?
parts: The five Ds are density, diversity, design, destination accessibility and distance to transit.
They describe different ways the built environment shapes travel choices.
Density alone cannot explain whether people can easily walk or use transit.
A dense neighborhood may still have disconnected streets and distant stations.

mnemonic.text: MUCH · MIX · STREETS · REACH · TRANSIT Density · Diversity · Design · Destination accessibility · Distance to transit.
lines: Density · Diversity · Design · Destination accessibility · Distance to transit.

fullParts: The D variables describe built-environment features associated with travel: density, diversity, design, destination accessibility and distance to transit.
They capture how much is nearby, the mix of uses, street connectivity, reachable destinations and access to transit stops.
Together they influence travel options; density alone is a weaker guide than considering the full setting.
Griddedness relates to design, while transit-oriented development combines several D variables in one planning approach.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: The five Ds describe how a neighborhood’s layout affects travel. Density is only one part of the picture.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A dense neighborhood can still be hard to walk around if streets do not connect and transit is far away.

name: Suburbanization
hook: People and jobs move toward the edge.
parts: Suburbanization is growth or movement toward a metropolitan area’s outskirts.
Cheaper land, better transport, housing preferences and policy can encourage it.
Homes and jobs become more spread out, often increasing car dependence.
Suburbanization is a process; sprawl describes a physical pattern.

mnemonic.text: Arrows OUTWARD. Homes and jobs move toward the edge.
lines: Homes and jobs move toward the edge.

fullParts: Suburbanization is the movement or growth of population and employment toward the outskirts of a metropolitan area.
Cheaper peripheral land, faster transport and housing preferences encourage outward development, shaped by public policy and unequal access.
It can decentralize jobs, increase car dependence and separate disadvantaged inner-city residents from employment.
It connects to spatial mismatch and polycentric development; it is a process, whereas sprawl describes a development pattern.

visuals.caption: Homes spread outward into suburbs. This photo shows one low-density pattern; suburbanization has other forms too.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Suburbanization is the movement or growth of homes and jobs toward a city’s outskirts.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A family moves outward for more space. Suburbanization is a process; sprawl is a physical pattern.

name: Pedestrian/Auto-Orientation
hook: Design for feet—or for cars?
parts: Pedestrian-oriented places support walking and staying; auto-oriented places prioritize driving.
Short crossings and nearby shops help walkers; wide roads and parking serve cars.
Design changes access, physical activity and street experience.
Compare walking five minutes for groceries with needing to drive.

mnemonic.text: Windshield view vs. walking view. Big roads and parking suit cars.
lines: Big roads and parking suit cars.

fullParts: Pedestrian orientation organizes places around walking and human-scale activity; auto-orientation prioritizes vehicle movement and access.
Short connected routes and nearby uses support pedestrians, while wide roads, parking and separated destinations favor cars.
These choices affect accessibility, physical activity and opportunities to linger or interact in public space.
Gehl connects auto-oriented streets to fewer optional activities, while TOD and traffic calming support pedestrian-oriented environments.

visuals.caption: A curb extension shortens the crossing and makes pedestrians more visible.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Pedestrian-oriented places make walking easy; auto-oriented places make driving the default.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Nearby shops and short crossings versus wide roads, large parking lots and long walks.

name: Jobs-Housing Mismatch
hook: The jobs move; the workers cannot follow.
parts: Jobs-housing mismatch separates workers from suitable jobs.
Jobs move outward while housing discrimination, transport and other barriers hold workers back.
Finding work becomes harder, and commuting costs rise.
A factory moves to the suburbs while its workers remain in the inner city.

mnemonic.text: WHERE: home here, jobs there. Picture a job moving outward while the worker cannot follow.
lines: Picture a job moving outward while the worker cannot follow.

fullParts: Jobs-housing mismatch is the spatial separation of workers, especially disadvantaged groups, from suitable employment.
Suburban job growth combines with housing discrimination, limited transport, hiring barriers and weak job information.
Workers face fewer accessible jobs, higher commuting costs and potentially lower employment or net earnings.
Ihlanfeldt emphasizes location barriers; Grengs’s modal mismatch shows why transport mode also matters within the same neighborhood.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Workers and suitable jobs are in different places, and barriers make the gap hard to cross.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A factory moves to the suburbs, while workers remain in the inner city with poor transport access.

name: Modal Mismatch
hook: Same home, different transport, different chances.
source: Grengs: Job Accessibility and Modal Mismatch in Detroit
parts: Modal mismatch means unequal job access through different transport modes.
The same address may offer good access by car but poor access by bus.
Residents without cars can be disadvantaged even near many jobs.
Grengs emphasizes MODE; spatial mismatch emphasizes WHERE homes and jobs are.

mnemonic.text: HOW: car key vs. bus pass. Keep the address fixed; swap the transport mode.
lines: HOW: car key vs. bus pass.
Keep the address fixed; swap the transport mode.

fullParts: Modal mismatch is unequal access to jobs arising from differences in available transport modes.
In Detroit, a neighborhood can offer good job access by car but poor access by public transit.
Neighborhood averages can hide disadvantages for residents without cars, whose complex daily trips may be difficult by transit.
It extends spatial mismatch: job proximity is insufficient, and accessibility must account for mode and competition for jobs.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A job can be easy to reach by car and hard to reach by bus. Modal mismatch is this gap between transport modes.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A workplace is 15 minutes away by car but 90 minutes by bus. MODE matters, not just distance.

name: Primal/Dual Accessibility
hook: Primal: how many? Dual: how long?
source: Course accessibility notes; Primal and Dual Access reference
parts: Primal accessibility counts opportunities within a fixed travel time.
Dual accessibility asks how long reaching a fixed number takes.
More opportunities improve primal access; less time improves dual access.
Compare “jobs within 30 minutes” with “minutes needed to reach 100 jobs.”

mnemonic.text: Primal = PILE. Dual = DURATION. Jobs within 30 minutes ↔ minutes to reach 100 jobs.
lines: Jobs within 30 minutes ↔ minutes to reach 100 jobs.

fullParts: Primal accessibility counts opportunities reachable within a fixed travel budget; dual accessibility measures the travel cost needed to reach a fixed number.
Primal might count jobs within thirty minutes, while dual asks how long reaching a specified number of jobs takes.
More opportunities improve the primal measure; less travel time improves the dual measure.
Both describe access to opportunities rather than speed alone, and both change with transport mode.

studyBlocks.label: Primal
studyBlocks.text: Fix the TIME; count reachable opportunities.

studyBlocks.label: Dual
studyBlocks.text: Fix the NUMBER of opportunities; measure travel time.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Jobs within 30 minutes versus minutes needed to reach 100 jobs.

studyBlocks.label: Better access means
studyBlocks.text: More opportunities for primal; less time for dual.

name: Cumulative/Competitive Accessibility
hook: Count the jobs—and the people competing.
source: Grengs; Shen’s competition adjustment discussed in the reading
parts: Cumulative accessibility counts reachable opportunities.
Competitive accessibility also accounts for the people seeking them.
Counting jobs alone can overstate a worker’s chances.
Ten openings mean something different with ten applicants than with a thousand.

mnemonic.text: Count the jobs—then the rivals. CUMULATIVE: count reachable openings.

fullParts: Cumulative accessibility counts opportunities within a travel threshold; competitive accessibility also accounts for people seeking those opportunities.
Two neighborhoods may reach the same number of jobs, but access is weaker where many more workers compete for them.
Simple job totals can therefore overstate labor-market opportunity for disadvantaged residents.
Grengs uses a gravity-based measure with competition adjustment, linking accessibility to spatial and modal mismatch.

studyBlocks.label: Cumulative
studyBlocks.text: Count opportunities you can reach.

studyBlocks.label: Competitive
studyBlocks.text: Also consider how many other people are seeking them.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Ten openings with ten applicants versus ten openings with a thousand applicants.

studyBlocks.label: Why it matters
studyBlocks.text: Many reachable jobs do not guarantee a good chance of getting one.

name: Travel Supply and Demand
hook: More lanes can attract more cars.
parts: Travel supply means transport capacity; demand means the trips people want to make.
A wider road makes driving easier and can attract more drivers.
New traffic can use up the extra capacity: induced demand.
For example, former bus passengers switch to cars and congestion returns.

mnemonic.text: More lanes can invite more cars. Picture a wider funnel attracting more water.
lines: More lanes can invite more cars.
Picture a wider funnel attracting more water.

fullParts: Travel supply is the capacity and service provided by transport networks; travel demand is people’s desire to make trips.
Land use creates trip needs, while travel time and cost affect where, when and how people travel.
Adding road capacity can attract additional driving, so induced demand may reduce congestion relief.
Congestion pricing manages demand, while transit-oriented development changes land use and travel options together.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: More road space can attract more driving, so congestion may return. This is induced demand.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A wider road saves time at first; people switch from buses to cars and fill it again.

name: Congestion Pricing
hook: Charge for crowded road space.
source: Course pricing notes; Dexter on travel demand
parts: Congestion pricing charges drivers for using busy roads, areas or times.
Some drivers change their route, time or transport mode.
Congestion can fall, but fairness depends on alternatives and how revenue is used.
Unlike adding lanes, pricing manages the demand for limited road space.

mnemonic.text: PRICE the PEAK. Charge for scarce road space at busy places or times.
lines: Charge for scarce road space at busy places or times.

fullParts: Congestion pricing charges drivers to use crowded road space, often varying by place or time.
The charge encourages some users to change routes, travel times, modes or whether they travel, reducing peak demand.
It can improve reliability and reduce congestion, but fairness depends on who pays and what alternatives or revenue uses exist.
Unlike road expansion that can induce more driving, it manages demand for limited transport capacity.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Congestion pricing charges for driving in busy places or times, encouraging some people to change trips.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A rush-hour charge may shift trips to another time or to transit. Fairness depends on alternatives and use of revenue.

name: Traffic Calming
hook: Change the street so cars slow down.
source: Course notes; FHWA Traffic Calming ePrimer
parts: Traffic calming uses physical design to reduce vehicle speeds.
Examples include speed humps, narrow lanes and raised crossings.
Walking, cycling and spending time near the street can become safer and more comfortable.
Contrast congestion pricing: street design changes speed; charging changes demand.

mnemonic.text: CALM the car with the street. Humps + narrow lanes + raised crossings.
lines: CALM the car with the street.

fullParts: Traffic calming uses street design to reduce vehicle speeds and improve conditions for people outside cars.
Speed humps, narrowed travel lanes, raised crossings and pedestrian refuges alter how drivers move through a street.
Slower traffic can improve safety and make walking, cycling and spending time near the street more comfortable.
It supports Gehl’s human-scale public spaces; unlike congestion pricing, it mainly changes street conditions rather than charging for road use.

visuals.caption: Raised cushions and a narrower passage make drivers slow down physically.
visuals.credit: The original uploader was Arpingstone at English Wikipedia.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Traffic calming makes drivers slow down through street design, such as humps, narrow lanes or raised crossings.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A speed hump physically slows cars. Congestion pricing instead changes demand by charging drivers.

name: Sedentary Disease
hook: Chair → car seat → office chair.
source: Wilson: planning, neighborhood health and riskscapes
parts: Sedentary disease refers to health problems linked to too little physical activity.
Car dependence, unsafe walking routes and limited recreation reduce daily movement.
These conditions can add to unequal neighborhood health burdens.
Wilson connects such risks to planning and environmental justice.

mnemonic.text: Sedentary → SEATED. Chair → car seat → office chair.

fullParts: Sedentary disease refers to health problems associated with prolonged inactivity, including increased risks of obesity and related chronic illness.
Car-dependent land use, unsafe walking routes and limited recreational access can reduce routine physical activity.
These conditions compound other neighborhood health burdens and can fall unevenly on disadvantaged communities.
Wilson connects health to planning and environmental justice; walkable mixed-use areas and traffic calming can support more active daily travel.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Too little everyday movement can contribute to disease. Car-dependent places and unsafe walking routes can make inactivity more likely.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: If even a short shopping trip requires driving, daily life offers fewer chances to walk.

name: Extreme Weather Events
hook: Same storm, different urban damage.
parts: Extreme weather includes unusually severe rain, heat or storms.
Pavement, drainage limits and exposed people or infrastructure affect the damage.
Floods, power failures and health risks can fall unequally across neighborhoods.
Remember hazard, exposure and vulnerability—not just how strong the storm is.

mnemonic.text: Same storm, different damage. Hazard + exposure + vulnerability.

fullParts: Extreme weather events are unusually severe conditions such as intense rainfall, storms or heat waves.
Urban pavement limits infiltration, drainage systems can be overwhelmed, and exposed infrastructure and vulnerable populations increase potential damage.
Flooding, heat stress and disrupted transport or electricity can impose unequal costs across neighborhoods.
This connects climate resilience to heat islands and environmental justice: risk depends on both the event and urban conditions.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Severe heat, rain or storms become more damaging when people and infrastructure are exposed and poorly protected.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: The same storm can cause very different harm depending on drainage, housing and who can evacuate.

name: Heat Islands
hook: Asphalt stores heat; trees provide shade.
parts: A heat island is an urban area warmer than its less-developed surroundings.
Heat-storing surfaces, limited vegetation and human activity raise temperatures.
Heat risks and cooling demand increase, especially affecting vulnerable residents.
Compare a sunny parking lot with a shaded street.

mnemonic.text: Asphalt frying pan; tree umbrella. Hard surfaces store heat; trees provide shade.
lines: Hard surfaces store heat; trees provide shade.

fullParts: An urban heat island is an urban area that is warmer than surrounding less-developed land.
Heat-absorbing surfaces, limited vegetation and shade, and heat released by human activities increase urban temperatures.
Higher heat raises health risks and cooling demand, putting pressure on electricity systems and especially affecting vulnerable residents.
Tree cover and cooler surfaces connect urban design to environmental justice and resilience during extreme heat events.

visuals.caption: Read the temperature line: built-up areas are warmer; greener areas are cooler.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Built-up areas can be warmer than their surroundings because hard surfaces store heat, greenery is limited and human activities release heat.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Compare a sunny asphalt parking lot with a shaded, tree-lined street.

name: Housing Shortage/Surplus
hook: Empty luxury flats do not solve every housing shortage.
parts: A housing shortage means too few suitable homes; a surplus means too many.
When demand grows faster than supply, rents tend to rise.
People may share homes, move farther away or pay more.
Luxury flats can sit empty while students still cannot afford rent.

mnemonic.text: Musical chairs, but with homes. Players = households; chairs = homes.

fullParts: A housing shortage means available housing falls short of demand; a surplus means supply exceeds demand in a particular market.
Supply depends on housing units, while demand depends on population, household formation and purchasing power.
Shortages put upward pressure on rents and overcrowding; surpluses can produce vacancies even while affordable housing remains scarce.
Building regulation shapes supply, while Rosen–Roback explains how migration can adjust demand across cities.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: A housing shortage means too few homes people need and can afford; a surplus means more homes than demand.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Empty luxury flats can exist alongside a shortage of affordable homes.

name: Filtering (Housing)
hook: Homes age; households may move up.
parts: Filtering happens when older housing becomes cheaper relative to newer housing.
Some households move into better homes, leaving older homes available.
Older buildings can therefore house lower-income residents.
Renovation and rising demand can reverse this process through gentrification.

mnemonic.text: Old housing rides DOWN an escalator. Aging homes may become relatively cheaper.
lines: Old housing rides DOWN an escalator.
Aging homes may become relatively cheaper.

fullParts: Housing filtering is the process through which older housing becomes available to lower-income households as its relative quality and price decline.
Buildings age while some households gain income and move to newer or higher-quality homes.
Older stock can provide affordable housing, although renovation, strong demand or demolition can interrupt this process.
Gentrification can reverse downward filtering by reinvesting in older neighborhoods and raising housing costs.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: As housing ages, it may become cheaper relative to new homes and available to lower-income households. This is filtering.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A once-expensive apartment becomes affordable as it ages; renovation and rising demand can reverse the process.

name: Building Regulation
hook: The same rulebook can protect—and exclude.
parts: Building regulation controls what, where and how people build.
Rules cover uses, lot sizes, height, parking and safety.
They can protect residents but also restrict housing supply and affordability.
Requiring large lots can exclude households unable to afford large homes.

mnemonic.text: A rulebook at the building site. One page protects safety; another limits size or uses.
lines: A rulebook at the building site.
One page protects safety; another limits size or uses.

fullParts: Building regulation consists of rules governing what, where and how development can be built, including zoning and building codes.
Use restrictions, lot sizes, setbacks, height limits, parking rules and safety standards shape the amount and form of construction.
Rules can protect health and safety, but restrictive requirements can limit housing supply and exclude lower-income households.
This connects Glaeser’s builder equilibrium to Wilson’s exclusionary zoning and to NIMBY-driven housing shortages.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Building rules control uses, size, location and safety. They can protect residents, but also limit housing supply and raise costs.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A large minimum lot size can make it impossible to build smaller, cheaper homes.

name: Gentrification
hook: The neighborhood improves—but who can stay?
parts: Gentrification brings wealthier residents and investment into a neighborhood.
Demand and renovation push up prices and change local businesses.
Existing residents may leave, struggle to stay, or lose their familiar surroundings.
A new café opens, but nearby tenants can no longer afford rent.

mnemonic.text: O–S–E: Out · Squeezed · Erased. Move out; costs squeeze; familiar culture disappears.
lines: Move out; costs squeeze; familiar culture disappears.

fullParts: Gentrification is neighborhood change associated with an inflow of wealthier residents and investment.
Increased demand, reinvestment and changing businesses raise housing costs and reshape local services and identity.
Existing residents may be displaced, remain under financial pressure, or experience cultural erasure even without moving.
It creates a planning dilemma: improving a neighborhood can undermine affordability, reversing filtering unless residents are protected.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Wealthier residents and investment move into a neighborhood, raising prices and changing local life. Existing residents may be displaced.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A renovated street gets new cafés, but longtime tenants can no longer afford the rent.

name: NIMBYism
hook: “Build it—but not beside my home.”
parts: NIMBY means Not In My Back Yard.
Residents oppose nearby projects because of concerns about traffic, property values or local conditions.
Opposition can restrict housing or move unwanted facilities elsewhere.
Someone supports affordable housing but opposes it on their own street.

mnemonic.text: “Yes—just not HERE.” Not In My Back Yard.

fullParts: NIMBYism means “not in my backyard”: residents resist a proposed development or facility near them.
Concerns about traffic, neighborhood character, property values or local burdens motivate opposition.
Opposition can constrain housing supply or shift unwanted facilities elsewhere, although specific local concerns may be legitimate.
It connects to building regulation, housing shortages and participatory planning that addresses local costs alongside wider needs.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: NIMBY means “Not In My Back Yard”: supporting an idea in general but opposing it nearby.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: “We need affordable housing—just don’t build it on my street.” Opposition can restrict supply.

name: Contact Hypothesis
hook: Liking one person may not change a prejudice.
source: Valentine: Living with Difference; Lecture 6a, slides 28–29
parts: The contact hypothesis says contact between groups can reduce prejudice.
Cooperation can help; competition and unequal power can get in the way.
Valentine shows that polite contact does not always produce respect.
“I like my neighbor, but their group is different” treats that person as an exception.

mnemonic.text: “My neighbor is the exception.” Liking one person ≠ respecting their whole group.
lines: Liking one person ≠ respecting their whole group.

fullParts: The contact hypothesis proposes that interaction between social groups can reduce prejudice and improve relations.
Meaningful, cooperative encounters may challenge stereotypes, while competition or unequal power can obstruct that change.
Valentine shows that proximity and politeness do not necessarily change wider beliefs: a liked individual may be treated as an exception.
Mixed neighborhoods and third places therefore create opportunities for contact without automatically producing respect or inclusion.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Contact between groups can reduce prejudice, but simply sharing space is not enough. Cooperation and equal standing help.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: “My neighbor is nice, but their group isn’t” shows how one friendly encounter may leave prejudice intact.

name: Sanitary Movement
hook: Make the city healthier before making it grand.
parts: The Sanitary Movement addressed disease and overcrowding in industrial cities.
Authorities improved water, sewage, waste disposal and housing conditions.
Public health became a reason for governments to plan and regulate cities.
Remember sanitation; contrast City Beautiful’s stronger focus on civic appearance.

mnemonic.text: SANITARY → SANITATION. Clean water IN; sewage OUT.

fullParts: The Sanitary Movement was a nineteenth-century response to disease and overcrowding in rapidly industrializing cities.
Public authorities improved water supply, sewage disposal, waste management and housing conditions to reduce health hazards.
It helped establish public health as a responsibility of urban government and a justification for planning and regulation.
It precedes City Beautiful’s emphasis on civic appearance and connects to Wilson’s concern with unequal environmental conditions.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: The Sanitary Movement made clean water, sewage, waste removal and healthier housing matters for city government.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Think “stop disease,” while City Beautiful puts more emphasis on impressive public design.

name: City Beautiful
hook: Beautiful outside—but where do people live?
parts: City Beautiful sought to improve cities through grand public design around 1900.
Planners such as Burnham promoted parks, boulevards and civic buildings.
Cities gained attractive spaces, but housing problems often received less attention.
Think of a beautiful city square surrounded by poor housing.

mnemonic.text: A city dressed for a parade. Monuments + boulevards + parks.
lines: A city dressed for a parade.

fullParts: City Beautiful was an American planning movement around 1900 associated with Burnham, Robinson and Olmsted’s landscape tradition.
It used monumental civic buildings, parks and broad boulevards to promote beauty, cleanliness and civic order.
It strengthened municipal planning and created lasting public spaces, but paid less attention to housing and everyday inequalities.
Garden City pursued broader social reform, while Jacobs later criticized planning that valued visual order over street life.

visuals.caption: Grand buildings and formal public space: beauty was meant to encourage civic pride.
visuals.credit: Nichols, H. D., 1859-1939 (artist); L. Prang & Co. (publisher)

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Make the city better by making it beautiful: grand civic buildings, parks and boulevards. Housing problems may receive less attention.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Chicago’s 1893 World’s Fair: impressive public spaces as a source of civic pride.

name: Garden City
hook: A working town inside a green belt.
parts: Howard’s Garden City combines town life with access to the countryside.
Homes, jobs and services sit inside a green belt; land ownership serves the community.
It aims to reduce overcrowding and improve living conditions.
It is a complete town, not just houses with gardens.

mnemonic.text: Town + country, held by a green BELT. Inside: homes + jobs + services.
lines: Town + country, held by a green BELT.

fullParts: Ebenezer Howard’s Garden City proposed small, self-contained towns combining urban opportunities with access to countryside.
Green belts limited expansion, while communal land ownership and a balance of homes, jobs and services supported the town.
It aimed to relieve industrial overcrowding and improve living conditions; later adaptations often emphasized suburban residential design.
Unlike City Beautiful’s civic aesthetics, Garden City linked physical design to social and economic reform.

visuals.caption: THREE MAGNETS: town + country → town-country. Combine urban opportunity with rural greenery.
visuals.credit: The original uploader was Marnanel at English Wikipedia.

visuals.caption: City + green belt + planned limits. Garden City means more than adding trees.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Howard’s Garden City combines town jobs and services with countryside access, a green belt and land held for community benefit.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A planned, complete town with limits on growth—not simply a suburb with gardens.

name: Neighborhood Unit (Clarence Perry)
hook: School in the middle, main roads at the edge.
parts: Perry’s Neighborhood Unit organizes housing around a school and community facilities.
Major roads form the boundary; shops sit near edge junctions.
Local streets and nearby parks support everyday neighborhood life.
Picture a plate: school at its center, main roads around its rim.

mnemonic.text: A school on a plate. School = center; main roads = rim.

fullParts: Clarence Perry’s Neighborhood Unit organizes a residential district around an elementary school and community institutions.
Major roads form its boundaries, shops sit near edge junctions, and interior streets provide local access with parks nearby.
The design aims to support neighborhood life and safer access to everyday facilities while separating through traffic.
It connects to Garden City traditions, but contrasts with Jacobs’s emphasis on continuous, interconnected mixed-use streets.

visuals.caption: School in the middle; major roads around the edge. Keep through-traffic outside.
visuals.credit: Clarence Perry / Committee on Regional Plan of New York and Its Environs

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Perry’s neighborhood has a school and community facilities near the center, major roads around the edge, and shops near edge junctions.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Picture a plate: school in the middle, main roads around the rim, local streets inside.

name: Modernism
hook: Sort the city into separate boxes.
parts: Modernism trusts expert planning to create an orderly, efficient city.
It separates functions such as housing, work and traffic.
Large projects may improve conditions but also break up communities.
Imagine housing towers far from shops; Jacobs favors mixed-use streets.

mnemonic.text: Sort the city into boxes. HOME / WORK / TRAFFIC / PARK.

fullParts: Modernism in planning sought a rational, functional city through comprehensive design, geometric order and limited ornament.
Planners separated land uses and reorganized buildings, open space and movement according to standardized principles.
It promised efficiency and healthier housing, but clearance and large-scale separation could disrupt neighborhoods and everyday street life.
Jacobs challenged this approach, arguing that mixed uses and informal street activity create a complex urban order.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Modernist planners try to make cities orderly and efficient by separating housing, work and traffic. Large projects can also disrupt communities.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Housing towers stand apart from shops and workplaces. Jacobs favors mixed-use streets instead.

name: Le Corbusier/Radiant City
hook: Radiant = rise: towers in parks.
parts: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City puts tall buildings in large open spaces.
It separates activities and replaces traditional streets with planned layouts.
It promises light and efficiency but can weaken everyday street life.
Contrast Broadacre: Radiant builds upward; Broadacre spreads outward.

mnemonic.text: RADIANT → RISE. Tall towers rising out of a park.
lines: Tall towers rising out of a park.

fullParts: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City was a modernist vision of a highly ordered city with tall buildings surrounded by open space.
It concentrated buildings, separated functions and circulation, and moved activity away from traditional streets into planned spaces.
It promised light, air and efficiency, but related urban-renewal approaches often weakened street continuity and displaced communities.
Contrast Wright’s dispersed Broadacre City and Jacobs’s defense of mixed-use streets and informal public supervision.

visuals.caption: Brasília illustrates related modernist principles: large open spaces, separated uses and major roads. It is not Le Corbusier’s original plan.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City puts tall buildings in open space and separates activities. It promises light and efficiency but can weaken street life.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Remember UP: towers in parks. Broadacre spreads OUT instead.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright/Broadacre City
hook: Broadacre = broad: spread out and drive.
parts: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Broadacre City spreads homes across the landscape.
Each family has roughly an acre, with cars connecting daily activities.
It offers space and nature but uses much land and depends on driving.
Contrast Le Corbusier’s concentrated towers in parks.

mnemonic.text: BROAD-acre → spread BROADLY. Picture a home, an acre and a car.
lines: Picture a home, an acre and a car.

fullParts: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Broadacre City proposed a decentralized settlement pattern, with roughly an acre of land for each family.
Dispersed homes, access to nature and automobile travel replaced the compact metropolitan center.
It promised household independence and space, but required extensive land and dependence on cars.
It contrasts with Le Corbusier’s concentrated Radiant City and helps interpret auto-oriented suburban development.

visuals.caption: BROAD = spread out. Notice the large plots and road-based layout in Wright’s sketches.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Wright’s Broadacre City gives families roughly an acre each and connects spread-out homes and activities by car.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Remember OUT: lots of land and driving. Radiant City builds UP instead.

name: Jane Jacobs (Death and Life of Great American Cities)
hook: Boundaries, eyes, and people throughout the day.
source: Jacobs: Uses of Sidewalks; Lecture 7a, slide 2
parts: Jane Jacobs argues that everyday street life creates order and safety.
Clear boundaries, eyes on the street and steady sidewalk use support informal supervision.
Residents, shopkeepers and passersby help watch the street.
A shopkeeper watches by day; residents watch at night. This contrasts with isolated superblocks.

mnemonic.text: B–E–H: Boundaries · Eyes · Hours. Clear edges; people watching; continuous sidewalk use.
lines: Clear edges; people watching; continuous sidewalk use.

fullParts: In The Death and Life of Great American Cities, Jane Jacobs defended everyday street life against top-down modernist planning.
Clear public–private boundaries, eyes on the street and fairly continuous sidewalk use support informal public supervision.
Mixed uses and daily sidewalk contacts can build safety and trust without relying only on formal policing.
Her “sidewalk ballet” contrasts with superblocks and separated functions, and connects to Gehl’s and Whyte’s human-scale observations.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Jacobs says ordinary street users help keep streets safe: clear public/private boundaries, “eyes on the street,” and people using sidewalks throughout the day.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Shopkeepers watch by day; residents and evening customers keep the street active later.

name: Urban Vitality
hook: Different reasons to visit, at different times.
parts: Urban vitality means active street life and the conditions supporting it.
Density, short blocks, mixed uses, varied building ages, access and no border vacuums help.
Steady activity can support shops, safety and everyday contact.
Offices bring daytime users; homes and restaurants keep the area active later.

mnemonic.text: People · Paths · Purposes · Prices · Access · Barriers Density · short blocks · mixed uses · building ages · access · no border vacuums.
lines: People · Paths · Purposes · Prices · Access · Barriers
Density · short blocks · mixed uses · building ages · access · no border vacuums.

fullParts: Urban vitality is visible street activity and the supportive built environment that sustains it.
Density, short blocks, mixed primary uses, varied building ages, accessibility and avoiding border vacuums bring different people out throughout the day.
Continuous use can support local businesses, informal supervision and sidewalk contacts, although density alone does not guarantee cohesion.
It develops Jacobs’s argument; Gehl asks whether activity includes optional and social life rather than only necessary trips.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Urban vitality means active street life. Mixed uses and a connected, accessible environment bring people out at different times.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Offices bring daytime customers; homes and restaurants keep the same street active at night.

name: Transit Oriented Development
hook: Put daily life within walking distance of transit.
parts: TOD puts dense, mixed-use development around transit stations.
Homes, shops and jobs connect through short blocks and walking routes.
People can meet more needs without driving.
Imagine buying groceries on the short walk home from the station—not just living beside a railway.

mnemonic.text: Train → groceries → home, on foot. A station surrounded by homes, shops and jobs.
lines: A station surrounded by homes, shops and jobs.

fullParts: Transit-oriented development concentrates dense, mixed-use, walkable development around transit stations, associated with Peter Calthorpe.
Short blocks, connected walking routes and nearby homes, shops and jobs make transit practical within roughly a ten-minute walk.
It can improve access and reduce car dependence when development and transport service work together.
TOD combines the D variables with Jacobs-style mixed use, contrasting with dispersed, auto-oriented development.

visuals.caption: Put daily destinations within walking distance of transit: station + density + mixed uses.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: TOD puts homes, shops and jobs around a transit station, with comfortable walking routes between them.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Get off the train, buy groceries and walk home. Living beside a railway alone is not enough.

name: Urban Acupuncture/Tactical Urbanism
hook: Try one useful change before a huge plan.
parts: Urban acupuncture uses small, targeted changes to improve city life.
Tactical urbanism often tests cheap, temporary projects.
People’s responses reveal what works before larger commitments.
Temporary seating can test a new public space. This connects to Lynch’s learning ecology.

mnemonic.text: A small needle, a targeted change. Acupuncture = act at a strategic point.
lines: A small needle, a targeted change.
Acupuncture = act at a strategic point.

fullParts: Urban acupuncture uses targeted interventions to improve city life; tactical urbanism often uses low-cost, temporary, small-scale projects.
Pop-up public spaces or temporary street improvements test ideas through local action rather than a complete master plan.
They can produce quick benefits and reveal how people use space, though wider problems may require lasting investment.
Lerner’s urban acupuncture connects to Lynch’s learning ecology: cities improve through adaptation and feedback.

visuals.caption: A small, inexpensive street intervention can change how a place feels and is used.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Urban acupuncture uses small, targeted changes to improve city life. Tactical urbanism often tries cheap, temporary changes before committing.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Add temporary seats and watch whether people stay. If they work, make the space permanent.

name: Jan Gehl (The Life Between Buildings)
hook: Good spaces make people want to stay.
parts: Jan Gehl studies everyday life between buildings.
Comfort, access, visibility and seating encourage people to linger.
Longer stays create more chances for casual, low-pressure contact.
A pleasant bench can turn a necessary walk into a pause and a conversation.

mnemonic.text: Gehl → 胶: people stick around. Comfort → stay → chat.

fullParts: Jan Gehl’s The Life Between Buildings focuses on how public-space design supports everyday pedestrian activity and interaction.
Comfort, visibility, access and places to linger encourage optional activities alongside necessary trips, allowing social activities to result.
Better spaces support longer stays and low-intensity contacts; car-oriented spaces often reduce activity to the bare minimum.
Gehl shares Jacobs’s interest in everyday contact, but does not treat extreme density or a grid as universally desirable.

visuals.caption: Places to sit make it easier to stay. Staying creates opportunities for social activity.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Gehl studies life between buildings. Comfortable, accessible places encourage people to stay, making casual contact more likely.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A pleasant bench turns a necessary walk into a pause and perhaps a conversation.

name: Necessary/Resultant/Optional Activities
hook: Need → choose → interact.
parts: Gehl separates necessary, optional and resultant social activities.
Going to work is necessary; sitting in a pleasant park is optional; chatting may result.
Poor spaces mainly retain necessary activity; better spaces encourage staying.
A busy sidewalk may simply contain commuters rushing through.

mnemonic.text: NEED → CHOOSE → CHAT. Need: walk to work. Choose: stop at a nice bench.
lines: Need: walk to work. Choose: stop at a nice bench.

fullParts: Gehl distinguishes necessary activities, optional activities and resultant or social activities in public space.
Necessary trips must happen, such as going to work; optional activities, such as lingering, depend more on favorable conditions; social activities arise from people’s presence.
Poor spaces mainly retain necessary activity, while comfortable spaces encourage staying and opportunities for contact.
The distinction explains why pedestrian counts alone cannot establish urban vitality or the quality of social experience.

visuals.caption: Sitting outside can be OPTIONAL; conversation can emerge as a RESULTANT / social activity.

studyBlocks.label: Necessary
studyBlocks.text: Things people must do, even in poor spaces: go to work.

studyBlocks.label: Optional
studyBlocks.text: Things people choose when conditions are inviting: sit in a park.

studyBlocks.label: Resultant / social
studyBlocks.text: Activity that emerges when people are together: a conversation.

studyBlocks.label: Remember
studyBlocks.text: Better space → more staying → more chances for contact. A busy sidewalk may only mean people rushing through.

name: Kevin Lynch (Learning Ecology)
hook: Help people learn and change their city.
parts: Lynch sees the city as a learning ecology.
People need spaces they can understand, use, reach and help control.
They can improve the city over time instead of following one fixed master plan.
Remember vitality, sense, fit, access and control; then ask about efficiency and justice.

mnemonic.text: Lynch → LEARN the city. Try → observe → adjust.

fullParts: Kevin Lynch described the city as a learning ecology in which people adapt their surroundings and change the rules of urban life.
Good form supports vitality, sense or legibility, fit, access and control, evaluated through efficiency and justice.
People can navigate, use and improve their city rather than depend on a once-and-for-all comprehensive plan.
This supports bottom-up planning and connects to urban acupuncture, contrasting with rigid modernist order.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Lynch treats the city as a place people can understand, use and improve through experience, rather than follow one perfect fixed plan.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Try a public-space design, observe how people use it, and change it. Ask who benefits and who has control.

name: William Whyte (Social Life of Small Urban Spaces)
hook: Watch what people do, not just what designers intend.
parts: William Whyte studied how people use small public spaces.
Seating, food, street access and other people encourage staying.
Useful, welcoming spaces support informal social life.
People may sit on steps while designed seats stay empty: actual use matters.

mnemonic.text: Whyte → WHY do people sit HERE? Watch actual choices: seats, food, access, other people.
lines: Whyte → WHY do people sit HERE?
Watch actual choices: seats, food, access, other people.

fullParts: William Whyte studied how people actually use small urban public spaces through systematic observation.
Comfortable seating, street connections, food and opportunities to watch others encourage people to stop and stay.
Successful spaces support informal sociability; designs that discourage unwanted users can also discourage everyone else.
His findings complement Jacobs’s street life and Gehl’s optional activities, while triangulation explains how shared attractions prompt conversation.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Whyte watched what people actually do in public spaces. Places to sit, food, street access and other people help attract users.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: People crowd onto steps while formal seats stay empty. Observe use instead of trusting the design on paper.

name: Triangulation
hook: Two strangers + a third thing = a conversation.
parts: Whyte’s triangulation happens when a shared attraction prompts strangers to interact.
Art, a performer or an unusual event gives them a common topic.
People who would otherwise stay separate may start talking.
Two strangers commenting on the same street performance form the triangle.

mnemonic.text: Two strangers + one shared thing = triangle. Person A → street performer ← Person B.
lines: Two strangers + one shared thing = triangle.
Person A → street performer ← Person B.

fullParts: Whyte’s triangulation occurs when a shared external stimulus gives strangers a reason to interact.
An artwork, performance or unusual event attracts their attention and provides a common topic.
People who would otherwise remain separate may exchange comments and briefly form a social connection.
It links public-space design to Gehl’s resultant activities, but Valentine reminds us that a brief encounter does not guarantee lasting respect.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Triangulation happens when a shared attraction gives strangers a reason to talk.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You and a stranger comment on the same street performer: person → performer ← person.

name: Ray Oldenburg (Third Places)
hook: Home first, work second, familiar hangout third.
parts: Oldenburg’s third places host regular, informal gatherings outside home and work.
They offer neutrality, equality, conversation, access, regulars, simplicity, playfulness and belonging.
Repeated meetings help build community ties.
Think of a familiar café; regulars and atmosphere matter more than attracting the biggest crowd.

mnemonic.text: 1 home · 2 work · 3 hangout. Third place = regulars + easy conversation.

fullParts: Ray Oldenburg’s third places are informal gathering places outside home and work that sustain regular social life.
They offer neutral ground, social leveling, conversation, accessibility, regulars, a low profile, playfulness and a sense of being at home.
Repeated voluntary encounters create belonging and everyday community ties.
Unlike approaches emphasizing foot traffic alone, Oldenburg stresses social character and regulars; this connects to Putnam’s concern about social capital.

visuals.caption: A familiar café can be a THIRD place: neither home nor work, but somewhere to meet regularly.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Oldenburg’s third places are informal gathering spots beyond home and work, where regulars meet and conversation feels easy.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A familiar café where you can linger and chat. Community comes from repeated contact, not just a big crowd.

name: Georg Simmel (“Blasé Man”/”Protective Organ”)
hook: The city is loud; the mind turns down the volume.
parts: Simmel’s blasé attitude is emotional reserve in response to city stimulation.
People filter the constant flow of noise, impressions and strangers.
This protective response can look like indifference.
Think of mental noise-canceling headphones. Goffman instead explains everyday interaction rituals.

mnemonic.text: Simmel → STIMULI → mental headphones. Too much city input → turn down emotional reactions.
lines: Too much city input → turn down emotional reactions.

fullParts: Georg Simmel’s blasé attitude describes emotional reserve developed in response to the intense stimulation of metropolitan life.
Individuals filter the constant flow of encounters and impressions, creating a psychological “protective organ.”
This helps people cope but can make urban relations seem impersonal or indifferent.
Unlike Goffman’s civil inattention, which concerns interaction rituals, Simmel emphasizes the mental response to urban overstimulation.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Simmel’s blasé attitude is a way to cope with city overload: people dull their reactions to constant noise, sights and strangers.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Mental noise-canceling headphones: seeming indifferent can be a form of self-protection.

name: Louis Wirth (“Collective Personality”)
hook: Size + density + diversity change social life.
parts: Wirth links urban life to large populations, density and heterogeneity.
People rely on specialized roles and cannot know everyone personally.
More limited, impersonal relationships become common patterns of urban behavior.
Contrast Jacobs, who sees these urban conditions as potential sources of neighborhood vitality too.

mnemonic.text: Wirth: S–D–H. SIZE + DENSITY + HETEROGENEITY.

fullParts: Louis Wirth argued that urbanism is a way of life shaped by large population size, density and social heterogeneity.
These conditions encourage specialized roles and more impersonal, segmented relationships among people who cannot know everyone personally.
Urban residents develop shared patterns of behavior, described in class as a collective personality, to navigate city life.
Contrast Jacobs, who emphasizes how these same conditions can support vitality, neighborhood contact and social cohesion.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Wirth links big, dense, diverse cities to more specialized and less personal relationships: no one can know everyone.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You know someone as your bus driver or cashier without knowing their wider life.

name: Erving Goffman (“Civil Inattention”)
hook: “I see you, but I will not bother you.”
parts: Goffman’s civil inattention is polite attention management among strangers.
A brief glance or nod is followed by looking away.
People acknowledge each other while protecting privacy.
Not staring at someone in an elevator is a social courtesy, not necessarily coldness.

mnemonic.text: Goffman → gaze OFF. Glance, then look away: acknowledge + privacy.
lines: Glance, then look away: acknowledge + privacy.

fullParts: Erving Goffman’s civil inattention is the polite management of attention among strangers sharing public space.
A brief glance, nod or small avoidance gesture acknowledges another person without inviting unwanted involvement.
These rituals preserve privacy and allow people to coexist comfortably in crowded settings.
Unlike Simmel’s psychological defense against overstimulation, civil inattention is an interaction practice; apparent ignoring can be social courtesy rather than hostility.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Civil inattention means briefly acknowledging a stranger, then looking away to give them privacy.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: In an elevator, a quick glance followed by looking away is polite—not necessarily unfriendly.

name: “Bowling Alone” (Robert Putnam)
hook: One bowler where a league used to gather.
parts: Putnam’s Bowling Alone argues that civic participation and social capital have declined.
Less involvement can weaken networks, trust and cooperation.
Communities may find collective action harder.
Aelbrecht adds that social life may move to newer places, such as malls, rather than simply disappear.

mnemonic.text: One bowler where a league used to meet. Putnam: weaker participation, networks and trust.
lines: One bowler where a league used to meet.
Putnam: weaker participation, networks and trust.

fullParts: Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone argues that social capital and community participation have declined in the United States.
Reduced involvement in associations and more solitary activity weaken networks, trust and habits of cooperation.
This can reduce the ties that support collective action and everyday community life.
Oldenburg emphasizes gathering places, while Aelbrecht qualifies Putnam’s account: interaction may shift from traditional organizations to newer spaces such as malls.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Putnam argues that declining civic participation weakens social capital: networks, trust and cooperation.
